lesson.title: unittest: Python's Built-in Test Harness
lesson.summary: The unittest module, part of Python's standard library, gives you a TestCase class with assertion methods and automatic test discovery, turning individual assert checks into an organized, repeatable test suite.
lesson.body:
You already know what unit testing means conceptually, checking a small piece of code in isolation against known expected results, and you already know that Python files can be organized as modules and imported. unittest is the standard-library module, meaning it ships with Python itself and needs no separate installation, that turns unit testing from a loose collection of assert statements into an organized framework with a consistent structure every test file can follow.

To use it, you subclass unittest.TestCase, and inside that class, you write methods whose names start with test_, unittest's test runner automatically discovers and runs every method named that way, you never have to call them by hand. Inside each test method, instead of a bare assert, you typically use one of TestCase's built-in assertion methods, such as self.assertEqual(actual, expected), which checks that two values match and, if they do not, produces a clearer failure message than a plain assert would, showing exactly what was expected versus what was actually returned.

```python
import unittest

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

class TestAdd(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_positive_numbers(self):
        self.assertEqual(add(2, 3), 5)

    def test_negative_numbers(self):
        self.assertEqual(add(-1, -1), -2)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()
```

Notice that final if __name__ == "__main__": guard from earlier in this unit, doing exactly the job it was built for: unittest.main() only runs, launching the test discovery and execution process, when this file is run directly, not if some other file imports it. Running this file directly, python test_add.py, executes both test_positive_numbers and test_negative_numbers. add(2, 3) returns 5, matching the expected value, and add(-1, -1) returns -2, also matching, so both tests pass. unittest prints one dot per passing test, followed by a summary. The output looks like this, with the exact timing number varying slightly from run to run:

```
..
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 2 tests in 0.000s

OK
```

If either assertEqual call had failed instead, unittest would print an F in place of the dot for that test, along with a detailed report showing which line failed and what value it actually got versus what was expected, then continue running the remaining tests rather than stopping at the first failure, letting you see every problem in one run instead of fixing them one at a time. That combination, automatic discovery of test_ methods, clear pass or fail reporting, and running the full suite even after a failure, is what makes unittest a genuine framework rather than just a script full of assert statements.
